newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania government to control privatisation agency.
newsitem.headline: Romania government to control privatisation agency.

text.p: Romania's government has decided to place the country's key privatisation agency under its direct control to speed up reforms, Reform Minister Ulm Spineanu said on Tuesday.
Spineanu told a news conference that the State Ownership Fund (FPS) would now be responsible to the centrist government elected last November, rather than parliament.

"We had expected a quicker pace of selloffs in the past two months," Spineanu said after a cabinet meeting. "We want to put greater responsibility on (FPS) employees or board members and make them implement the government's reform strategy."
Since its creation in 1992, the FPS has sold some 3,000 of more than 6,500 companies in which it held 70 percent of shares. It has been frequently accused of irregularities and of delaying sell-offs.

Spineanu cited studies showing that 50 companies which received FPS funds to make them more profitable before privatisation had in fact increased their losses. Managers of state-run companies, he said, were concealing unprofitability.
"Chaos in data on companies' performance makes it impossible to take concrete decisions," Spineanu said.
The government's overall privatisation plan calls for the private sector to account for 80 percent of gross domestic product by the year 2000 against 52 percent last year.
A new FPS president, Sorin Dimitriu, was elected early this year in a reshuffle replacing all 17 members on its board following last November's election defeat of ex-communists.
Spineanu also said that 40 percent of privatisation receipts would become state budget revenues. Half would go towards regional development and environment protection.

Earlier this year Dimitriu pledged to put 75 percent of the economy in private hands within two years, through offerings through the stock exchange, the over-the-counter market and direct negotiations for attractive equities.

Western and Romanian analysts accused the ousted government of stalling reforms and doing little to encourage foreign investment in Romania, eastern Europe's second largest market after Poland. Direct foreign investment since 1989 stands at $2.3 billion, far lower than most other ex-communist countries.
